papers.title_in_file: Computing with only a few light particles
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc educational web lesson explaining photons, number states versus coherent states, antibunching, and why weak coherent states are used as a testbed for few-photon photonic computing.

assertions.value: The lesson states that the energy of a photon of a given wavelength is fixed, and that the amount of light energy changes with the number of photons, so a brighter pulse of the same color contains more photons than a fainter one.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 3
quotes: The amount of energy that a photon of a given wavelength (which determines its color) has is fixed, but the amount of energy can be changed by changing the number of photons.
A brighter pulse of light contains more photons than a fainter one which is the same color.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states this as a basic definition-level fact of the setting.

assertions.value: The lesson gives lower energy use as an obvious motivation for computing with fewer photons.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 3
quotes: This gives an obvious motivation to use fewer particles - it requires less energy.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor lesson states its motivation without a measurement.

assertions.value: The lesson states that if light were not composed of discrete particles, the rate of energy emission from hot objects would be infinite, a paradox it names the ultraviolet catastrophe, and that discretization fixes it.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 1
quotes: If light wasn't composed of discrete particles, the rate of energy emission would be infinite, an apparent paradox known as the ultraviolet catastrophe.
This discretization fixes the apparent paradox
assertions.certainty_reason: Textbook physics restated in a vendor lesson without derivation or citation.

assertions.value: The lesson defines a number state as a pulse of light containing an exact number of photons, and states that with a perfect measurement device a number state with two photons always gives a result of exactly two.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 4
quotes: A pulse of light which is represented by a number state contains an exact number of photons.
Assuming a perfect measurement device, a number state with two photons will always give a result of exactly two.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines the term in the text.

assertions.value: The lesson states that a coherent state has a fixed amount of energy and so a fixed average photon number, but that measurements are noisy even with a perfect device, with outcomes random as if each photon were added independently of the others (Poisson statistics).
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 4
quotes: There is a different kind of state, known as a coherent state, and these states have a fixed amount of energy.
This means there will be a fixed amount of photons on average, but measurements will be noisy.
The outcomes are random as if each photon has been added independently of the others (mathematically this is known as Poisson statistics ).
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines coherent states and their measurement statistics in the text.

assertions.value: The lesson states that number states can only be built with integer numbers of photons, while coherent states can have an average photon number that is not an integer, and even less than one.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 4
quotes: It is therefore only possible to build number states with integer numbers of photons, but coherent states can be made with an average number of photons that are not an integer, and even less than one.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states this as a property of the two state types it defines.

assertions.value: The lesson states that, no matter how few photons a weak coherent state has, it behaves like a classical pulse of light until the final measurement, which must measure an integer number of photons.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, paragraph 4
quotes: A remarkable fact about weak coherent states is that no matter how few photons they have, they still behave like a classical pulse of light until the final measurement, which must measure an integer number of photons.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement in a vendor lesson with no derivation in the page.

assertions.value: The lesson states that weak coherent states are relatively easy to produce, and so provide a good starting point for developing technology.
assertions.anchor: Photons, the particles that makeup light, last sentences
quotes: Weak coherent states are relatively easy to produce, so as we see later, they provide a good starting point for developing technology.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own development approach.

assertions.value: The lesson states that, for a perfect detector, detecting a photon can only make it more likely, not less, that another is detected soon after under classical light, so that a beam of constant brightness gives the most spread out detections and any intensity profile only makes the distribution more bunched.
assertions.anchor: It is easier to see quantum mechanics with fewer particles, paragraph 2
quotes: For a perfect detector, detecting a photon can only ever make it more likely that we detect another one soon after, not less.
no matter what the intensity profile looks like, the probability peaks at a time difference of zero and the most spread out they can be is if the intensity is uniform.
assertions.certainty_reason: Illustrated by an animation in a vendor lesson; no proof in the text.

assertions.value: The lesson defines antibunched light as light in which detecting a photon makes it less likely to detect another one right after, and states that evenly spaced single light particles are the way to make light very antibunched, indicating the quantum nature of single photon states. It cites an early experiment that observed antibunching in light from a quantum source.
assertions.anchor: It is easier to see quantum mechanics with fewer particles, paragraph 2
quotes: There is a kind of light known as antibunched light that is less likely to detect a photon right after detecting another one.
This early experiment was able to observe antibunching in light from a quantum source.
It should be intuitive that evenly spaced single light particles are the way to make light very antibunched indicating the quantum nature of single photon states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The experiment is cited by link text only; the lesson gives no detail of the result.

assertions.value: The lesson states that, as the number of photons in a number state increases, the second-order coherence approaches, but never quite reaches, the minimum value that classical light can take.
assertions.anchor: It is easier to see quantum mechanics with fewer particles, paragraph 3
quotes: This states that as the number of photons in a number state increases, this quantity approaches, but never quite reaches, the minimum value that classical light can take.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a derivation or a value in the text.

assertions.value: The lesson states that adding more particles, even in a very quantum way, masks the fact that they are discrete particles, and that quantum states with a single photon or few photons are an excellent environment to realize quantum effects. It uses an analogy of grains of sand.
assertions.anchor: It is easier to see quantum mechanics with fewer particles, paragraph 3
quotes: Adding more particles, even in a very quantum way, masks the fact that they are discrete particles.
Quantum states (as opposed to coherent states, and including but not limited to number states) with a single or few photons are an excellent environment to realize quantum effects
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by analogy in a vendor lesson, with no measurement.

assertions.value: The lesson states that weak coherent states do not have the desirable quantum properties of single photons, but behave like single photons in many other ways, for example being very low energy and so hard to detect and hard to use for non-linear interactions.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: While they don't have the desirable quantum properties, weak coherent states will behave like single photons in many other ways.
they are very low energy and are therefore hard to detect and implement non-linear interactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states the limit of weak coherent states directly in this paragraph.

assertions.value: The lesson states that weak coherent states are an excellent tool to understand what can be done and to contribute to developing devices while ensuring scalability, and that they let the team see at an earlier stage of hardware development what works and what does not.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: An advantage of relatively easy-to-prepare weak coherent states is that they provide an excellent tool to understand what we can do and to contribute to the development of our devices, ensuring scalability.
We can therefore use these states to understand what works and what doesn't at an earlier stage in hardware development.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own development method.

assertions.value: The lesson states that nonlinear optics can convert weak coherent states into more quantum states, and that a nonlinear system that starts with weak coherent states can transform them into more interesting quantum states over time.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: Additionally, nonlinear optics can also convert weak coherent states into more quantum states.
so a nonlinear system that starts with weak coherent states can transform them into more interesting quantum states over time.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement in a vendor lesson with no derivation or data on the page.

assertions.value: The lesson states that the nonlinear effects underlying QCi's technology have been experimentally demonstrated by its team to make an excellent source of single photons. The page gives no data for this result and links to it.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: The nonlinear effects that provide the foundation of our technology have been experimentally demonstrated by our team to make an excellent source of single photons .
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own product; the page carries no measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not say what source quality was measured or how, so the word excellent is unquantified here.

assertions.value: The lesson states that working with weak coherent states makes engineering much easier and allows rapid testing, and that this ability to look ahead lets the team design different elements of its architecture independently and understand encodings and protocols on a large scale early on.
assertions.anchor: Weak coherent states as a testbed and starting point, paragraph 1
quotes: However, working with weak coherent states allows for a setting where engineering is much easier, and allows us to rapidly test what works and what doesn't.
This ability to "look ahead" allows us to design different elements of our architecture independently, and gain an understanding of encodings and protocols on a large scale early on.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own design process.

papers.what_it_is: A short Quantum Computing Inc web lesson page claiming quantum computers threaten public-key cryptography and that QKD alone is insufficient, listing three use cases.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Public-Private Key scheme is constructed assuming the intractability of some mathematical problems, such as finding large integers' prime factors (RSA) or computing integer pairs satisfying the curve equation (ECC).
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: In a nutshell, PPK is constructed assuming the intractability of some mathematical problems like finding large integers' prime factors (e.g., in RSA), or computing integer pairs satisfying the curve equation (e.g., in ECC).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors state that PPK-based protocols are generally considered secure because no efficient algorithm is known to solve those problems on current digital computers.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: The PPK-based protocols are generally considered to be secure as there is no known efficient algorithm to solve those math problems in current digital computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors claim that quantum computers will defeat current cryptographic algorithms and decrypt data while it is being transmitted.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: Quantum computers will defeat current cryptographic algorithms and decrypt data while it is being transmitted.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors claim that quantum computers will be able to defeat cryptographic hash functions by implementing fast search algorithms.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: However, quantum computers will be able to defeat this approach by implementing fast search algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors claim that quantum computers will defeat authentication algorithms, making data transmission vulnerable to interception or diversion and enabling malicious parties to penetrate the communication chain.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: Quantum computers will defeat authentication algorithms thereby making data transmission vulnerable to being intercepted/diverted or enabling malicious parties to penetrate the communication chain.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors claim that an adversary armed with a quantum computer can easily forge digital signatures and fake certificates.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: An adversary armed with a quantum computer can easily forge digital signatures and fake certificates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors state that random numbers are a vital ingredient in all cryptographic algorithms, that random number generators produce encryption keys, and that increasing randomness or entropy is essential to the future of secure communications.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: Random number generators are used to produce encryption keys.
Increasing the randomness/entropy is essential to the future of secure communications.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors claim that quantum computers' ability to crack encryption and authentication protocols will invalidate the premises on which privacy-preserving computing schemes rely.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: will invalidate the premises on which privacy-preserving computing schemes rely
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors state that, despite many efforts to replace PPK with post quantum cryptography methods, none has been proven secure against future quantum algorithms.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: Even though many efforts have been invested to replace PPK using post quantum cryptography methods, none has been proven to be secure against future quantum algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Key Distribution is not enough to defend communication networks in the quantum era, because it solves only the distribution of encryption keys and guarantees only the security of data-in-transit even when running ideally.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: QKD focuses on solving only one problem, the distribution of encryption keys.
Even if running ideally, a QKD-based network can only guarantee the security of data-in-transit.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The authors state that authentication, verification and digital signatures still rely on classical cryptography in a QKD network and are thus vulnerable to quantum computer attacks.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: authentication, verification, and digital signatures, still rely on classical cryptography and are thus vulnerable to quantum computer attacks
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: QCi states that it is building an end-to-end quantum solution to defend the security of the digital world against quantum computer attacks.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: QCi is building an end-to-end quantum solution to defend the security of our digital world against quantum computer attacks with the following use cases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.
assertions.reader_inference: No product, protocol or result is described on the page.

assertions.value: The page lists secure multi-party computation as a use case: distrusted parties compare and perform a secure computation on their combined data without revealing their personal data.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: A pool of distrusted parties wish to compare and perform a secure computation on their combined data without revealing their perspective personal data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The page lists user authentication as a use case: a credit card user proves identity by showing knowledge of the secret password without revealing it.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: A credit card user must prove her identity by showing she knows the secret password without revealing her actual password.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

assertions.value: The page lists private blockchain transaction as a use case: a user performs a zero-knowledge proof to process a blockchain transaction while remaining anonymous.
assertions.anchor: Cybersecurity under quantum computer threats, p.1
quotes: A user wishes to perform zero-knowledge proof to process a transaction on a blockchain while remaining anonymous.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without evidence in a vendor lesson page.

papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc educational web lesson arguing that integer problems are hard and that integer (including binary) problems map onto its Dirac solvers.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear optimization under linear constraints becomes NP-hard when the variables are restricted to integers, and that this model is known as integer linear programming.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer Optimization, web lesson (single page)
quotes: In fact, they become NP-hard
This is a famous model known as integer linear programming
assertions.certainty_reason: A textbook result stated without proof or citation on the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The NP-hardness of integer linear programming is a standard result, but this page neither proves it nor cites a source.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for continuous variables, interior point methods can solve linearly constrained linear optimization efficiently, in the sense of polynomial time.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer Optimization, web lesson (single page)
quotes: it can be proven that these methods, known as " interior point methods " can solve this kind of problem efficiently in the sense of polynomial time
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the page attributes to a proof elsewhere (a linked lesson), not shown here.

assertions.value: The authors state that rounding a non-integer point can go two ways per variable, that the number of possibilities doubles each time a variable is added (16 directions to round in four dimensions), and that the number of points to check grows exponentially.
assertions.anchor: Section Why is integer hard?, web lesson (single page)
quotes: the number of possibilities doubles each time a variable is added
with 16 possible directions to round
the number of points to check grows exponentially
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative argument for naive rounding, given without a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument covers only exhaustive checking of the points adjacent to a continuous optimum; it is an intuition, not a hardness proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that no known algorithm is efficient for finding the most optimal integer solution, and that finding one would show that P=NP.
assertions.anchor: Section Why is integer hard?, web lesson (single page)
quotes: none that we know of so far are efficient for finding the most optimal solution
if one were found, this would show that P=NP
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of the state of knowledge, without citation.
assertions.reader_inference: The implication holds for NP-hard problems in general; the page states it for integer linear programming without argument.

assertions.value: The authors state that a family of algorithms using clever rounding, known as LP relaxations, provides a powerful class of approximation algorithms.
assertions.anchor: Section Why is integer hard?, web lesson (single page)
quotes: a family of algorithms which use clever rounding are known as LP relaxations and provide a powerful class of approximation algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement without citation or approximation guarantees.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear optimization without additional constraints is either trivial or unbounded.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer Optimization, web lesson (single page)
quotes: Without additional constraints, these problems are either trivial or unbounded.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated with a short informal argument in the text, not a formal proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The page states this for non-negative variables, as set up in the preceding sentences.

assertions.value: The authors state that the equation setting the sum of the cubes of two positive integers equal to the cube of a third positive integer has no solution, and that this can be proven with advanced mathematics.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer problems tend to be harder, web lesson (single page)
quotes: it can be proven that there is no solution
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the page asserts without proof or citation.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the exponent-three case of Fermat's Last Theorem; the page does not name it.

assertions.value: The authors state that finding two factors of a given number is trivial without restrictions but becomes hard when the factors must be integers, and that this hardness is the basis of much of modern cryptography.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer problems tend to be harder, web lesson (single page)
quotes: this problem again becomes hard if we require that X X X and Y Y Y be integers
In fact, this kind of problem being hard is the basis of much of modern cryptography
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement without proof or citation.
assertions.reader_inference: Integer factoring is not known to be NP-hard; the page uses hardness loosely here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cube equation and factoring examples are not optimization problems, though they could be converted to optimization problems, and that integer problems tend to be hard and are therefore a natural paradigm for QCi's solvers.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer problems tend to be harder, web lesson (single page)
quotes: While neither of the problems discussed so far are optimization problems (although they could be converted to optimization problems)
integer problems tend to be hard, and therefore are a natural paradigm for QCi's solvers
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing the fit of its own product to a problem class.
assertions.reader_inference: The page says integer problems tend to be hard; it does not say all instances are hard.

assertions.value: The authors state that a linear inequality constraint has a natural quadratic expression: a squared penalty term with a non-negative slack variable and a large positive constant, which is zero when a suitable slack value exists and otherwise incurs a large penalty.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer linear programming and Dirac, web lesson (single page)
quotes: linear constraints have a very natural quadratic expression
can be found to make the expression zero. But if it cannot, a large penalty is incurred.
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard penalty construction described informally; no bound on the constant is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not say how large the penalty constant must be for the penalized problem to share its optimum with the constrained one.

assertions.value: The authors state that their Dirac hardware is designed to solve quadratic unconstrained problems, that Dirac provides a more powerful model than integer linear programming because the objective can also contain quadratic terms, and that it can implement even higher order interactions.
assertions.anchor: Section Integer linear programming and Dirac, web lesson (single page)
quotes: our Dirac hardware is designed to solve quadratic unconstrained problems
Dirac provides a more powerful model than integer linear programming, since nothing prevents the objective function from also containing quadratic terms.
It can also implement even higher order interactions
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own product; no performance data on the page.
assertions.reader_inference: More expressive is not more efficient; the page gives no solution-quality or speed result.

assertions.value: The authors state that a variable can be limited to a maximum value by adding a single additional slack variable and one squared term.
assertions.anchor: Section Binary problems on a higher-than-binary solver, web lesson (single page)
quotes: We can constrain a variable to take a maximum value of m m m , by adding a single additional variable.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction stated without proof; it follows the slack penalty of the previous section.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a non-negative variable the expression X times the square of (X minus one) is zero if and only if the variable equals 0 or 1, and takes a positive value for other integer points.
assertions.anchor: Section Binary problems on a higher-than-binary solver, web lesson (single page)
quotes: will be zero if and only if X i = 0 X_i=0 X i = 0 or X i = 1 X_i=1 X i = 1
and will take a positive value for other integer points
assertions.certainty_reason: The property follows by direct inspection of the expression, stated with its condition (non-negative variable) in the section.
assertions.reader_inference: The expression is cubic in the variable, yet the page calls the constraint quadratic (it says it can be accomplished with a quadratic constraint if we restrict to integers). The zero and positivity property holds as stated; the quadratic label is the page's wording and does not match the printed degree.

assertions.value: The authors state that a variable can be constrained to binary values without adding a slack variable, so a binary problem with n variables, a QUBO for example, can be mapped to an integer solver with n variables.
assertions.anchor: Section Binary problems on a higher-than-binary solver, web lesson (single page)
quotes: We can therefore constrain a variable to take binary values without adding an additional slack variable.
can be mapped to an integer solver with n variables
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing how problems map onto its own solver.
assertions.reader_inference: The saving counts variables only; the binary-enforcing term has higher degree than the quadratic form the hardware is described as solving, so the claim of no overhead depends on the higher order interactions the page mentions elsewhere.

assertions.value: The authors state that an integer solver can do everything a binary solver can do, plus much more.
assertions.anchor: Section Binary problems on a higher-than-binary solver, web lesson (single page)
quotes: an integer solver can do everything a binary solver can do, plus much more!
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own product class.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that solving problems over an integer domain tends to be harder than over continuous variables, that integer problems are therefore an important and powerful setting for their hardware, and that general integer problems can be restricted to binary using simple constraints without extra variables.
assertions.anchor: Section Conclusion, web lesson (single page)
quotes: A key feature of these problems is that it tends to be harder to solve problems over an integer domain rather than continuous variables.
integer solving is an important and powerful setting for our hardware to work in
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor summarizing the fit of its own hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson contains no experiments; every statement is argued informally or stated without citation.

papers.title_in_file: Interaction graph connectivity - Quantum Computing Inc
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc web lesson arguing that full interaction-graph connectivity matters for optimization hardware, using treewidth to bound how large a fully connected problem a quasi-planar chip can embed.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because light moves and light pulses can easily be divided into parts, realizing full connectivity in optical devices is conceptually straightforward.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 1
quotes: since light is constantly moving and light pulses can easily be divided into parts, realizing full connectivity is conceptually straightforward.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of the connectivity of optical devices; the lesson cites the literature rather than proving it.

assertions.value: The authors describe a coupling scheme in which a small part of one light pulse is pulled off and added to another pulse, and they point to a 2016 paper's figure 1 as an example.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 1
quotes: An effective scheme can be to simply pull off a small part of one pulse and add it to another (see figure 1 of this paper from 2016 for example).
assertions.certainty_reason: A scheme attributed to other work; the lesson does not test it.

assertions.value: The authors state that interactions can also be simulated by classical feedback (measuring, then using a laser to return the feedback pulse), that this approach disrupts entanglement, and that it gives an easy way to experiment with large-scale highly-connected devices.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 1
quotes: The interactions can also be simulated using classical feedback, by measuring and using a laser to return what the feedback pulse should be.
Although such an approach disrupts entanglement, it provides an easy way to experiment with large-scale highly-connected devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit (entanglement is disrupted) in its own description of the feedback approach.

assertions.value: The authors claim that most, if not all, real industrial optimization problems have highly connected interactivity graphs, and that the overhead of mapping them to less-connected hardware can be huge.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 1
quotes: Most, if not all, real industrial optimization problems have highly connected interactivity graphs, and the overhead of mapping to less-connected hardware can be huge
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim with no evidence given in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: No survey or citation is given for the 'most, if not all' statement.

assertions.value: The authors report a back-of-the-envelope estimate that, under realistic constraints, a highly connected problem with a few hundred variables takes on the order of 10,000 qubits on a non-fully-connected chip architecture, and that a typical 10,000 variable problem would need on the order of 100 million physical qubits.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 1
quotes: a highly connected problem with a few hundred variables (still small in terms of optimization problems), will take on the order of 10,000 qubits to map.
More typical 10,000 variable problems would require the order of 100 million physical qubits to map.
assertions.certainty_reason: A rough estimate the authors call a quick back-of-the-envelope calculation; its inputs (the TRIAD-based qubit estimate with d=6 and d=20) are only shown in a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer does not carry the figure that shows the estimate for d=6 and d=20, so the figures cannot be checked from the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that on their hardware one qubit is one variable of an optimization problem, because any qubit or qudit can interact with any other, so a binary variable maps to a single qubit and a discrete variable maps to a single qudit.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 2
quotes: Our hardware does not have this issue, one qubit is one variable in an optimization problem.
A single binary variable maps to a single qubit, and a single discrete variable maps to a single qudit.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that if interactions are restricted and a problem is not naturally compatible with the restrictions, the only way to solve it is a one-to-many mapping, in which each variable is mapped to many qubits or qudits.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 2
quotes: then the only way to do it is through a one-to-many mapping, where each variable is mapped to many qubits or qudit.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim stated without proof at this point; the treewidth section gives the supporting argument.

assertions.value: The authors state, as the headline result, that for realistic restrictions from placement on a two-dimensional chip the size of a highly-connected problem that can be solved goes as the square root of the size of the device, whereas on their hardware it scales directly as the size.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 2
quotes: The headline result here is that for realistic restrictions from placement on a two-dimensional chip, the size of a highly-connected problem that can be solved goes as the square root of the size of the device, whereas on our hardware it scales directly as the size.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson argues it by a sketch of a tree decomposition that is not a formal proof, and it rests on the unproved treewidth monotonicity claim; the hardware half is a vendor statement.
assertions.reader_inference: The scaling argument is informal. It assumes an interaction range much smaller than the graph size, a condition the lesson states only in the treewidth section.

assertions.value: The authors examine the TRIAD method, proposed in a cited paper, for mapping a complete interaction graph to quasi-planar hardware, using as examples d=6 and d=20, where d is the number of qubits each qubit can interact with, and they note the estimate is not necessarily accurate when n is close to d.
assertions.anchor: Interactions, paragraph 2
quotes: we examine the TRIAD method to map a complete interaction graph to quasi-planar hardware proposed in this paper
in this example we consider as examples d=6 and d=20
note that this estimate is not necessarily accurate when n
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the setup and the caveat of its own example in this passage.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer garbles the closing math of the caveat (a repeated 'n' and 'd' form), so the quote stops before the approximation sign.

assertions.value: The authors define the interactivity graph as the graph of what can directly interact with what, and say that on their analog hardware any qubit or qudit can be made to interact with any other, so the graph is a complete graph.
assertions.anchor: Interaction graphs, paragraph 1
quotes: we can think of an interactivity graph, which is the graph of what can directly interact with what, as a graph with edges joining all of the nodes
any qubit or qudit can be made to interact with any other one.
assertions.certainty_reason: The definition is general, but the full connectivity of the vendor's analog hardware is a vendor statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that in superconducting circuits each variable often corresponds to a physical circuit element with a size constraint, and coupler circuits can only be so long, so the interaction graph cannot be fully connected and is instead quasi-planar, in which a node can interact only with nodes nearby in a 2D plane.
assertions.anchor: Interaction graphs, paragraph 1
quotes: the interaction graph for such devices cannot be fully connected, it must instead be a type of graph we call quasi-planar
In a quasi-planar graph nodes (representing the qubits), can only have edges (be allowed to interact) with others which are nearby in a 2D plane.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines quasi-planar in this passage; the application to superconducting circuits is the paper's stated scope.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson applies the quasi-planar model to superconducting circuits as a whole; it does not discuss devices with longer-range couplers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the interaction graph of a problem is read from its QUBO (or QUDO) representation by assigning a node to each variable and an edge whenever there is a non-zero off-diagonal element in the QUBO matrix.
assertions.anchor: Interaction graphs of optimization problems, paragraph 1
quotes: We can assign a node to each variable, and then assign edges between them whenever there is a non-zero off-diagonal element in the QUBO matrix.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the construction in this passage.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the conventional traveling salesperson formulation, with a variable for each city at each tour position, the city-once and one-city-at-a-time constraints and the distance penalties make the interaction graph highly connected, though not quite fully connected.
assertions.anchor: Interaction graphs of optimization problems, paragraph 3
quotes: While not quite fully connected, it is clear that the interaction graph representing a traveling salesperson problem is highly connected.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argued claim with no count of edges or measured example.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most used method to map a more connected graph to a less connected one is minor embedding, in which connected groups of qubits (graph minors) are strongly coupled together so they act as a single variable, and that it is not the only method.
assertions.anchor: Mapping to a less connected graph
quotes: The most used method is one called minor embedding , where connected groups of qubits ("graph minors" in technical terms) are strongly coupled together so they act as a single variable.
Technically minor embedding isn't the only way to map a more connected graph to a less connected one
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines minor embedding as it uses the term.

assertions.value: The authors state the rules of a tree decomposition: nodes connected by an edge in the original graph must appear together in some node of the new graph, all new-graph nodes holding the same original node must be connected, the new graph must be a tree with no loops, and the goal is to minimize the number of original nodes in the largest new node.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 2
quotes: Any nodes connected by edges in the original graph must appear in the same node at least once in the new graph
The new graph must be a tree, it cannot have any loops
The goal is to minimize the number of nodes of the original graph which appear in the "largest" node of the new graph
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines tree decomposition in this passage.

assertions.value: The authors define treewidth as the number of variables in the largest node of the tree decomposition minus one, a convention chosen so that a graph without loops (a tree) has a treewidth of one.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 3
quotes: this property is defined as the number of variables in the largest node of the tree decomposition minus one.
to guarantee that a graph without loops (a tree) will have a treewidth of one.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines treewidth in this passage.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is not possible to map a graph with a given treewidth into a graph with a smaller treewidth, and they offer it as intuitive without proving it in the lesson.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 3
quotes: The key property of treewidth is that it is not possible to map a graph with a given treewidth into a graph with a smaller treewidth, this is hopefully somewhat intuitive.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a key property with an appeal to intuition and no statement of conditions or proof; the embedding notion it applies to is not defined in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The precise statement (for example, that a graph minor cannot have larger treewidth than the graph it is a minor of) is not given; the claim is stated for 'any' mapping, which the lesson does not define.

assertions.value: The authors state that dynamic programming algorithms can solve certain NP-hard problems efficiently on graphs with low treewidth even with many variables, and that a mapping from high to low treewidth graphs would show P=NP.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 3
quotes: certain dynamical programming algorithms can solve NP-hard problems on graphs with low treewidth efficiently, even if the problem involves a large number of variables.
This implies that if a mapping were possible from high to low treewidth graphs, it would show P=NP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without citation or proof in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The implication holds only if the mapping is efficient (polynomial time) and preserves the problem; the lesson does not state these conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that finding the most optimal tree decomposition is in general a computationally hard problem, though in some cases simple arguments about the treewidth are possible.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 3
quotes: In general finding the most optimal tree decomposition is a computationally hard problem, but in some cases it is possible to make simple arguments about the treewidth.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit on its own method in this sentence.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most optimal tree decomposition of a fully connected graph puts every node in the same new node, making its treewidth n-1 for a graph of size n.
assertions.anchor: Treewidth of different graphs, paragraph 1
quotes: this makes the treewidth of a fully connected graph of size n equal to n-1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is given with a one-line argument, and the conditions of a formal theorem are not quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the standard result that a complete graph on n nodes has treewidth n-1.

assertions.value: The authors say that a highly connected graph should also have a treewidth close to the number of nodes, and that they do not prove it here.
assertions.anchor: Treewidth of different graphs, paragraph 1
quotes: I won't prove it here, but it should also be intuitively clear that a highly connected graph should also have a treewidth close to the number of nodes.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim the paper states it does not prove.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Highly connected' is not defined, so the claim carries no stated condition.

assertions.value: The authors describe a tree decomposition for a quasi-planar graph that divides it into overlapping rows, each of twice the interaction range and spaced by the interaction range, so that each row overlaps only with the row above and the row below and the resulting graph has no loops.
assertions.anchor: Treewidth of different graphs, paragraph 2
quotes: we divide the graph into overlapping rows which each have a size of twice the interaction range, and spaced by the interaction range.
Each of these rows will overlap only with the row above it and the row below it so therefore the graph resulting from this decomposition will have no loops.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction argued in prose, not stated as a theorem with its conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that for an n-by-n quasi-planar graph, where the interaction range is much smaller than the graph size, the number of nodes in each row is proportional to n while the total number of nodes is proportional to n squared, so the size of highly connected graphs that can be mapped scales as the square root of the size of the hardware interactivity graph.
assertions.anchor: Treewidth of different graphs, paragraph 2
quotes: For an n-by-n quasi-planar graph (where the interaction range is much smaller than the graph size), the number of nodes in each row is proportional to n but the total number of nodes is proportional to n 2
therefore the size of highly connected graphs which can be mapped scales as the square root of the size of the hardware interactivity graph if it is quasi-planar.
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal scaling argument, not a theorem; it relies on the unproved claim that mapping cannot reduce treewidth.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument gives an upper bound on treewidth of order n from the row decomposition. The conclusion about the largest mappable problem follows only through the no-reduction property of treewidth.

assertions.value: The authors work an example with a quasi-planar graph of n=25 nodes, for which they show the treewidth cannot be more than 9, and they state this implies it is impossible to map a fully connected problem with more than 10 nodes to it by any method.
assertions.anchor: Treewidth of different graphs, final paragraph (figure not in text layer)
quotes: In this example, the graph has n=25 nodes, but we have shown the treewidth cannot be more than 9.
This treewidth implies that it is impossible to map a fully connected problem with more than 10 nodes to it by any method.
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked illustration whose decomposition is in a figure the text layer does not carry; the 'any method' conclusion rests on the unproved no-reduction property.
assertions.reader_inference: A fully connected problem of 10 nodes has treewidth 9, so the bound of 9 is consistent with the stated limit of 10 nodes, given the no-reduction property.

assertions.value: The authors state that a more optimal decomposition of the n=25 example graph is possible and that its treewidth is actually only 6, and they pose as an exercise finding the decomposition whose largest grouping holds only 7.
assertions.anchor: Treewidth of different graphs, final paragraph
quotes: In this example, the graph has n=25 nodes
Note that a more optimal (but more complicated to draw) decomposition is possible, but this simple one demonstrates the necessary scaling. The treewidth of this graph is actually only 6.
Can you figure out the corresponding decomposition with the largest grouping containing only 7?
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without the decomposition or a proof in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: A treewidth of 6 means a largest grouping of 7 nodes, which matches the closing question. The 25-node graph is probably a 5-by-5 grid, whose treewidth is known to be 5, not 6; the lesson does not say which quasi-planar graph it uses, so this cannot be checked from the text.

papers.title_in_file: Ising Models, what are they? From physics to computer science
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc web lesson that explains Ising models, the QUBO mapping, spin glasses and why quantum mechanics does not make NP-hard optimization easy.

assertions.value: The authors define an Ising model as a set of spins that each take one of two values, and state that its energy is written in terms of whether spins are the same or different.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: which can take values of + 1 +1 + 1 or − 1 -1 − 1
The energy of an Ising model is written in terms of whether spins are the same or different
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the Ising model in the section 'What are Ising models?'.

assertions.value: The authors write the energy of an Ising model as a sum over pairs of spins, each weighted by an entry of a matrix J that tracks the interactions.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: E = ∑ i , j J i j σ i σ j
where J is a matrix to keep track of the interactions
assertions.certainty_reason: The page gives the energy expression in the section 'What are Ising models?'.

assertions.value: The authors state that a slightly more general Ising model, often used in practice, adds terms that penalize the values of individual spins, with h a vector.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: A slightly more general version of the Ising model is often used in practice, which includes terms that penalize values of individual spins
where h is a vector
assertions.certainty_reason: The page gives the general form in the section 'What are Ising models?'.

assertions.value: The authors state that Ising models were first developed in the early twentieth century as a model for magnetism.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: Ising models were first developed in the early 20th century as a model for magnetism
assertions.certainty_reason: A historical statement the page links to the original paper but does not argue.

assertions.value: The authors state that early physics studies used highly structured Ising models (spins in a line, or on a grid with equal strengths), and that such models are not very interesting from a computing perspective.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: Early physics studies were interested in highly structured Ising models
but are not very interesting from a computing perspective
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that Ising models become interesting for computing when the interaction matrix J is allowed to be arbitrary, because such Ising models can be mapped to hard combinatorial optimization problems, the class known as NP-hard optimization problems.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: Where Ising models become interesting for computing is when the interactions, described by the matrix J J J , are allowed to be arbitrary
can be mapped to hard combinatorial optimization problems. This is a particularly interesting class of problems known as NP-hard optimization problems
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement; the page gives only the max-cut example as support.

assertions.value: The authors state that placing J values where edges exist in a graph, and zeros elsewhere, makes the lowest energy state of the Ising model the maximum cut of the graph, which they describe as one of the early problems shown to be NP-hard.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: if we place J J J values where edges exist in a graph, and all zeros elsewhere, then the lowest energy state of an Ising model will be the maximum cut of the graph
one of the early problems shown to be NP-hard
assertions.certainty_reason: The page asserts the mapping without a derivation; the NP-hardness is cited by link only.
assertions.reader_inference: The sign of J needed for the minimum to equal the maximum cut is not stated on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that physical systems tend to naturally yield interactions based on variables being the same or different, so Ising models can map important optimization problems and can be engineered into physical systems, and for this reason they naturally arise when quantum systems are used to solve optimization problems.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: physical systems tend to naturally yield interactions based on variables being the same or different
For this reason, Ising models naturally arise when using quantum systems to solve optimization problems
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors offer two possible reasons that physical models are expressed as Ising models and not as QUBO: the Ising model is symmetric under inverting its two spin values and physical laws tend to be derived from symmetries, and physicists who derive models are familiar with Ising models. They state the reason is probably a mixture of both.
assertions.anchor: Section 'What are Ising models?', p.1
quotes: One answer is that the Ising model is symmetric in terms of inverting the
physical laws tend to be derived from symmetries
In truth, the reason is probably a mixture of the physical/mathematical and psychological explanation
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors say they do not fully answer the question.
assertions.reader_inference: The page labels this an open question that it does not fully answer.

assertions.value: The authors define a QUBO (quadratic unconstrained binary optimization) model as almost identical to an Ising model except that its variables take the value zero or one.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models
These models are almost identical to Ising models except that they involve variables x x x , which take the value 0 0 0 or 1 1 1
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines QUBO in the section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models'.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with the substitution x = (1 - sigma)/2, a QUBO can be mapped into an Ising model (at least the version with the h terms) and the reverse, and that adding constants to the energy does not change which state has the minimum energy, so constants can be ignored in practice.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: it is clear that a QUBO can be mapped into an Ising (at least the more general version involving h h h ) and vice-versa
adding constants to the energy has no effect on which state has the minimum energy
assertions.certainty_reason: The page shows the algebraic mapping in the equation of the section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models'.
assertions.reader_inference: The page writes the substitution with a minus sign, x = (1 - sigma)/2; the displayed equation uses a one-quarter factor with sigma terms.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QUBO interaction adds to the energy only if both variables take the value one, which is natural in computing (penalizing that case is a disjunctive clause with two negated literals) but does not tend to arise physically.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: the QUBO interactions only add to the energy if both take the 1 1 1 value
but does not tend to arise physically
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state, as Quantum Computing Inc, that their software provides both the QUBO and the Ising formulation, and that the QUBO form may be the preferred way to program for many users.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: may be a preferred way to program for many users (our software provides both formulations)
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own software.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Ising formulation more closely describes what their hardware is doing, that the dynamic range (the ratio of the largest and smallest magnitude non-zero coupling) will generally differ between the QUBO and Ising settings, and that the Ising value is the one that is relevant for device performance.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: Since the Ising formulation more closely describes what the hardware is doing
the dynamic range (the ratio of the largest and smallest magnitude non-zero coupling) will generally be different in the QUBO and Ising settings
However, the Ising value is the one that is actually relevant for device performance
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own hardware; no measurement is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that Ising systems with randomly chosen couplings show glassy behavior: below a certain temperature they tend to become stuck in local energy minima, configurations where small changes cannot lower the energy but large changes could find a better solution. They call such random Ising systems spin glasses.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Spin Glass', p.1
quotes: one particular context is the setting where couplings are chosen randomly
once they cool down below a certain temperature, they tend to become stuck in what are known as local energy minima
These random Ising systems are often called
assertions.certainty_reason: An author description of known physics, with no evidence in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The last quote ends before the term in quote marks, to keep quote marks out of the quote.

assertions.value: The authors state that glassy behavior has a deep connection to problems being difficult to solve, and that transitions to glassy states are how these problems become hard for physical systems, or for algorithms that simulate physical systems such as simulated annealing.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Spin Glass', p.1
quotes: This behavior has a deep connection to problems being difficult to solve
These transitions to glassy states are how these problems become hard to solve for physical systems or algorithms that simulate physical systems like simulated annealing
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that conventional thinking in computer science is that certain problems should be hard to solve by any method, which they call the P not equal to NP conjecture, and that this conjecture puts constraints on the physics of a system to which optimization problems are mapped.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Spin Glass', p.1
quotes: conventional thinking in computer science is that certain problems should be hard to solve using any method
the conjecture that these problems would be hard for all computational methods puts constraints on the physics of the system
assertions.certainty_reason: An author argument by reasoning, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors argue by counter-example that if Ising systems never behaved as spin glasses and reached thermal equilibrium quickly at any temperature, then mapping an NP-hard problem to the system and simulating cooling to a very low temperature would solve the problem quickly and would show that P equals NP.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Spin Glass', p.1
quotes: Let us assume for the moment that Ising systems do not ever behave as spin glasses
Therefore if we can simulate cooling to a very low temperature quickly, then we can solve the optimization problem quickly
If it could reach equilibrium at a low temperature quickly, our simulation would have shown that P = N P P=NP P = NP
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal argument by the authors, with no formal proof in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument is informal: it does not state the conditions on the mapping or on the error probability.

assertions.value: The authors state that the only two ways out of showing that P equals NP would be that the system could not be simulated efficiently (which they say is not true because classical spin systems are relatively easy to simulate), or that the real physical system takes a very long time to reach thermal equilibrium. They state that the second is what happens in practice, with equilibration times much longer than the age of the universe not uncommon.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Spin Glass', p.1
quotes: if we couldn't simulate the system efficiently (which we know isn't true because classical spin systems are relatively easy to simulate)
it takes a very long time for the real physical system being simulated to reach thermal equilibrium
equilibration times much longer than the time the universe has existed are not uncommon
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without citation or data in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that physical glasses, including silicate window glass, are in practice never truly in thermal equilibrium, and that they have rich and poorly understood physics with deep connections to fundamental issues in computer science.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Spin Glass', p.1
quotes: which in practice are never truly in thermal equilibrium
These humble materials have rich and poorly understood physics and deep connections to fundamental issues in computer science
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that quantum mechanics does not change the picture much: it is likely to find better solutions faster for combinatorial optimization problems (which they say has been observed in condensed matter systems), but the general consensus is that it will not make these problems easy.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Conclusion', p.1
quotes: At a high level, quantum mechanics doesn't actually change this picture much
the general consensus is that it will not make these problems easy
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion, with the 'general consensus' not cited in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The page links the observation in condensed matter systems but names no source in its text.

assertions.value: The authors state that physicists have shown that quantum systems also exhibit spin glass phases, even though quantum mechanics is not generally easy to simulate classically.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Conclusion', p.1
quotes: quantum mechanics is not generally easy to simulate classically
physicists have shown that quantum systems do indeed also exhibit spin glass phases
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the page attributes to other physicists by link.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum mechanics has the promise of allowing equilibration to occur much faster and greatly improving performance, which they say broadly agrees with the theoretical computer science view that quantum hardware may be revolutionary in making optimisation much faster while the problems stay hard.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Conclusion', p.1
quotes: quantum mechanics does have the promise of allowing the equilibration to occur much faster and greatly improve performance
quantum hardware may be revolutionary in making the solving of optimisation much faster, but the problems will still be hard
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes the promise of its field and product class; no result is given.
